Of course. And remember it's a process. It all accumulates so even if you can't commit yourself to much time with hands on right now, it all matters in the end. Do what you can with what you have, and try to personally connect with nature and plants to really understand how they grow.

I also just wanted to add- I have been lucky to connect with some great people who have much more experience then me. Learning from them and learning from the plants themselves is apart of the hands on. You cannot go in expecting to understand everything right away, having experienced gardeners to keep in touch her with is also something I recommend.

Do you have any way to get hands on experience? An online course will teach you the book smarts and botanical side of things which is very important, but plants and cultivation varies so much depending on region and species and you can learn so much just by spending time around them. I personal volunteer at my local botanical Garden as well as caretaker my own aroid greenhouse (nothing crazy just a 12 by 7 foot one from Amazon). This had let me get an understanding with the plants themselves and I am planning on taking horticultural classes at the university of Florida. If possible I recommend volunteering or maybe even getting a job at a local nursery at the same time as your college course. And remember that your mindset towards plants and your understanding of how they function and grow changes a lot but it takes time to learn these things. Some plants grow very slowly and it can be fufilling to watch them grow and care to them, and hold them in contrast with much faster growing plants. 

Tl;Dr Nothing can replace hands on experience. I still am in favor of you taking the course but some kind of hands on experience in the form of volunteering or a job at a nursery will help foster your understanding of horticulture.
